title: Merge two sorted arrays in-place.
shortTitle: Merge Two Sorted Arrays In-Place: Fill From the Back
keyPoints: Merge from the back by placing the larger of the two tails into the last empty slot, moving backward through the first array.
The first array has spare capacity at its end sized to hold both arrays, so writing from the back never overwrites unread elements.
Three pointers are used: i at last real element of array one, j at last element of array two, k at last slot of array one.
Stop when the second array is exhausted; remaining first-array elements are already in their correct positions.
The invariant is that the write pointer k is always at or ahead of the read pointer i, guaranteeing no clobbering.
Runs in O(m + n) time with O(1) extra space since no separate output array is needed.
For financial records, compare with BigDecimal compareTo so transaction amounts are ordered exactly.

s1_definition.oneliner: Merge from the back, placing the larger of the two tails into the last empty slot, moving backward.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **In-place merge** – takes a first array with spare capacity at its end and a second sorted array, merging the second into the first so the result is sorted, without allocating a separate output array.
- **Write from the back** – three pointers start at the last real element of each input and the very end of the first array; the larger tail element is placed at the write position, moving backward.
- **O(m + n) time, O(1) space** – each element is compared and placed exactly once with no extra allocation.
- **Stop condition** – stop when the second array is fully consumed; leftover first-array elements are already in place.
- **Safety invariant** – the write pointer is always at or ahead of the read pointer in the first array, so no element is overwritten before it is placed.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India keeps Rajesh's transactions in a ledger sized with spare blank rows at the bottom, and Priya's smaller sorted ledger must be merged in so the whole thing stays in date order, without opening a brand-new ledger book. Instead of inserting from the top and shoving everyone down, the clerk fills from the bottom-most blank row upward, each time copying whichever of the two next-largest dates is bigger, so nothing ever gets overwritten before it is placed.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Merging two sorted arrays in-place takes a first array with spare capacity at its end and a second sorted array and merges the second into the first so the whole thing stays sorted, without allocating a separate output array. You do it in O(m + n) time and O(1) space by writing from the back: three pointers start at the last real element of each input and the very last slot of the first array, and you copy the larger of the two compared tails into the write position, moving backward.

Writing from the back rather than the front is the entire trick. Merging from the front would overwrite elements of the first array that have not been merged yet, but the back of the first array is exactly its free capacity, so writing there never clobbers a value you still need. The invariant that the write pointer is always at or ahead of the read pointer guarantees safety.

The subtle correctness point is when to stop. You stop as soon as the second array is exhausted, not when both are, because any elements left in the first array are already sitting in their correct positions. Getting that asymmetry right is what separates a correct implementation from a common buggy one.

In a banking project at the National Bank of India, this is used to consolidate Priya's transactions into Rajesh's pre-sized ledger array so a statement generator can read one sorted list, with no second allocation even for large ledgers.

Remember one sentence: Write from the back of the spare capacity, placing the larger tail element each time, and stop when the second array is exhausted.
